Exploratory Bayesian analysis provided evidence in favor of the null hypothesis of no intergroup bias in selfish dishonesty (BF10 = 0.08), indicating the data were approximately 13 times more likely under the null than the alternative hypothesis. One explanation might be that selfish dishonesty primarily engages self-interest motives, which may be less susceptible to group identity cues. Finally, the effect was statistically non-significant across both Democrats (73.9% vs. 73.8%, p = .988) and Republicans (73.4% vs. 70.4%, p = .411). See Figure 1.

Dishonesty beliefs.

We predicted that participants would overestimate outgroup dishonesty more than ingroup dishonesty. We calculated belief-reality differences by subtracting the actual dishonesty rate in the relevant condition from each participant's estimate. As predicted, the general belief measure showed that participants overestimated outgroup dishonesty (M = 10.39, SD = 25.40) more than ingroup dishonesty (M = 1.11, SD = 23.49), t(1175) = 6.51, p < .001, d = 0.38, 95% CI [0.26, 0.50]. The second measure, which specified pairing with an opposing-party voter, showed the same overall pattern. Exploratory analyses indicated that Democrats showed greater overestimation of outgroup than ingroup dishonesty on both measures, whereas Republicans showed no significant difference on either measure (see Supplemental Materials, Section F, for both measures and party-level analyses).

EXPERIMENT 2: INTERGROUP BIAS IN COALITIONAL DISHONESTY

This pre-registered experiment examined how intergroup bias might affect coalitional dishonesty-the decision to lie to benefit an ingroup or an outgroup member without any personal benefit-testing whether people would be more likely to engage in selfless dishonest behavior to benefit political ingroup members than outgroup members. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions in a between-subjects design, where the beneficiary of their dishonest behavior was systematically varied.

The hypotheses, design, sample size, exclusion criteria, and analyses were pre-registered (see https://aspredicted.org/64cb-4k49.pdf) before data collection. No deviations from the preregistration occurred. Exploratory analyses not included in the pre-registration are clearly labeled.

Method

Design, participants, and power. We recruited 900 Democrat-and 897 Republicanidentifying U.S. American participants on Prolific. As pre-registered, we excluded participants flagged as duplicate or fraudulent by Qualtrics (n = 54) and those who failed the attention check (n = 33). This left us with a final dataset of 1,710 participants (Mage = 43.4, SD = 14.3; 796 male, 896 female, 18 other). A sensitivity analysis using G*POWER showed that the achieved sample size could detect an effect size of w = .10 and larger with 90% statistical power and α = .05. Procedure. As in Experiment 1, after providing informed consent and completing the attention check, participants completed demographic measures. Participants completed the same die-roll paradigm. Unlike Experiment 1, the experimental manipulation was implemented in the bonus mechanism, and participants' own payoffs were not affected by their responses.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions. In the "Affect Ingroup Condition", if they reported that they guessed correctly, a same-party voter would receive a $0.75 bonus, and if they reported they guessed incorrectly, there would be no bonus. In the "Affect Outgroup Condition", if participants reported that they had guessed correctly, an opposing-party voter would receive a $0.75 bonus, and if they reported they guessed incorrectly, there would be no bonus for anyone. In the "Ingroup Over Outgroup Condition", if participants reported that they had guessed correctly, a same-party voter would receive a $0.75 bonus, and if incorrectly, an opposing-party voter would receive a $0.75 bonus. In all three conditions, participants were told the outcome would not affect their personal payoffs and that their identity would remain anonymous.

Participants then completed the same individual-level measures as Experiment 1. They were also asked, in separate randomized questions, what percentage of Democratic and Republican Party voters completing the same study would falsely state they guessed correctly.

Responses were incentivized with an additional $1 bonus for the closest five guesses.

Results

Behavioral dishonesty.

The coalitional hypothesis predicted that people would be more likely to engage in selfless dishonest behavior to benefit an ingroup member than an outgroup member. Consistent with this hypothesis, a chi-square test revealed that the proportion of correct guesses in the ingroup condition (61.9%) was significantly higher than in the outgroup condition (52.8%), χ 2 (1, N = 1,147) = 9.74, p = .002, OR = 1.45, 95% CI [1.15, 1.84]. This effect of 9.1 percentage points corresponds to participants being 17.3% more likely to report correct guesses to benefit an ingroup member than an outgroup member.

We also predicted that people would be more likely to lie to benefit an ingroup member at the cost of an outgroup member than to benefit an outgroup member at the cost of the experimenter. A chi-square test revealed that the proportion of correct guesses in the Ingroup Over Outgroup Condition (60.0%) was significantly higher than in the outgroup condition (52.8%), χ 2 (1, N = 1,135) = 6.04, p = .014, OR = 1.34, 95% CI [1.06, 1.70].

Finally, we predicted that people would lie to benefit ingroup members even if it harmed the outgroup. A binomial proportion test revealed that the proportion of correct guesses within the Ingroup Over Outgroup Condition (.60; 95% CI [.56, .64]) was significantly higher than the .50 baseline, p < .001, BF10 = 4,698. The ingroup condition (61.9%) was also substantially above chance (p < .001, BF10 = 727,247). Importantly, the outgroup condition (52.8%) was not below 50%, providing no evidence for outgroup-directed spiteful dishonesty. The ingroup and Ingroup Over Outgroup conditions also did not significantly differ (χ²(1) = 0.42, p = .516), indicating that the opportunity to simultaneously harm the outgroup did not increase coalitional dishonesty beyond helping the ingroup alone. These results indicate that intergroup bias in coalitional dishonesty is driven by ingroup love rather than outgroup hate.

Exploratory analyses revealed that among Republicans, the ingroup vs. outgroup effect was significant (63.3% vs. 53.1%, χ²(1) = 6.11, p = .013, φ = .10). Among Democrats, the effect was also in the same direction (60.5% vs. 52.5%, χ²(1) = 3.84, p = .050, φ = .08). The Party × Condition interaction was not significant (χ²(1) = 0.15, p = .700), indicating comparable effect sizes across parties.

For the ingroup-over-outgroup vs. outgroup comparison, Democrats showed a significant effect (61.9% vs. 52.5%, χ²(1) = 5.17, p = .023, φ = .10), while Republicans showed a directionally consistent but non-significant effect (58.1% vs. 53.1%, χ²(1) = 1.43, p = .232, φ = .05). In the ingroup-over-outgroup condition, both Democrats (61.9%, p < .001) and Republicans (58.1%, p = .008) reported correct guesses significantly above the 50% chance baseline. See Note that we have substantially less statistical power to detect interaction effects or conduct subgroup analyses, which leads us to suggest that these exploratory analyses should be interpreted with caution.

Dishonesty beliefs.

As in Experiment 1, we predicted and found that people overestimated dishonest behavior among outgroup members more than ingroup members (M = 35.12, SD = 25.70 vs. M = 25.84, SD = 23.89), t(1709) = 17.19, p < .001, d = 0.42, 95% CI [0.37, 0.46].

An exploratory 2 (Affiliation) × 3 (Behavioral Condition: ingroup vs. ingroup-overoutgroup vs. outgroup) × 2 (Belief Target: ingroup vs. outgroup, within-subjects) mixed ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of belief target, F(1, 1704) = 313.30, p < .001, η²p = .155, and a significant Belief Target × Affiliation interaction, F(1, 1704) = 12.02, p < .001, η²p = .007. Both Democrats (d = 0.51) and Republicans (d = 0.33) overestimated outgroup dishonesty more than ingroup dishonesty, though this asymmetry was stronger among Democrats. See Figure 3. dishonesty across all three experimental conditions, though the asymmetry was stronger among Democrats. Positive values indicate overestimation; the dashed line at zero indicates perfect calibration. Panels display Democrat and Republican participants separately. Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.

Unlike Experiment 1, the coalitional context revealed intergroup bias in dishonesty beliefs from both parties. Importantly, the three-way Belief Target × Affiliation × Condition interaction was significant, F(2, 1704) = 49.08, p < .001, η²p = .054, indicating that how much each party overestimated outgroup dishonesty relative to ingroup dishonesty varied across the experimental condition they were in (see Supplemental Materials, Table F3, for all cell means and party-level decompositions).

EXPERIMENT 3: SELFISH VERSUS COALITIONAL DISHONESTY

This pre-registered experiment examined how intergroup bias affects both selfish and coalitional dishonest behavior, testing whether people are more likely to engage in selfish dishonest behavior to personally benefit at the cost of an outgroup member than an ingroup member, and whether people are more likely to engage in selfless dishonest behavior to benefit an ingroup member than an outgroup member.

The hypotheses, design, sample size, exclusion criteria, and analyses were pre-registered (see https://aspredicted.org/f857-7wmk.pdf) before data collection. No deviations from the preregistration occurred. Exploratory analyses not included in the pre-registration are clearly labeled in the manuscript.

Method

Participants and power. We recruited 1,204 Democrat-and 1,201 Republican-identifying U.S. American participants on Prolific. Participants received a base payment of $0.75. As pre-registered, we excluded participants who failed the attention check (n = 62). This left us with a final dataset of 2,343 participants (Mage = 41.1, SD = 13.7; 1,150 male, 1,169 female, 24 other). A sensitivity analysis using G*POWER showed that the achieved sample size could detect an effect size of w = .10 and larger with 90% statistical power and α = .05.

Procedure. Using a 2 (dishonesty type: selfish vs. coalitional) × 2 (target: ingroup vs. outgroup) between-subjects design, we randomly assigned participants to one of four conditions.

The goal was twofold: replicate the results of Experiments 1 and 2, and directly compare selfish and coalitional dishonesty within a single factorial design. After providing informed consent and completing the attention check, participants responded to demographic measures. Participants were informed they had been paired with another participant, with either an ingroup or outgroup signal based on political affiliation, following the same logic used in Experiments 1 and 2.

In the selfish dishonesty conditions, as in Experiment 1, if participants self-reported having guessed correctly, they would receive a $0.75 bonus; if incorrectly, their paired participant would receive the $0.75 bonus. In the coalitional dishonesty conditions, as in Experiment 2, if participants self-reported having guessed correctly, their paired participant would receive a $0.75 bonus; if incorrectly, their paired participant would not receive any bonus.

After completing the honesty task, participants completed the same individual-difference measures as Experiments 1 and 2. In addition, participants responded to six moral judgment measures assessing cheating aversion, anticipated guilt, moral wrongness, justification, deservingness, and expected reciprocal cheating, each on 1-7 scales (see Supplemental Materials for exact wording). Participants were also asked in a random order what percentage of Democratic and Republican Party voters, when paired with a voter from the paired participant's political party, would falsely state they guessed correctly. Five participants with the closest guesses would receive an additional $1 bonus.

Results

Selfish dishonesty.

Replicating Experiment 1, a chi-square test comparing selfish dishonesty at the cost of an ingroup vs. outgroup member showed that the proportion of correct guesses in the ingroup condition (74.7%) was not significantly different from the outgroup condition in Experiment 3 (72.7%), χ 2 (1, N = 1,154) = 0.59, p = .443, OR = 1.11, 95% CI [0.85, 1.44]. Exploratory Bayesian analysis provided evidence in favor of the null hypothesis (BF10 = 0.09), with the data being 11 times more likely under the null than the alternative hypothesis.

Coalitional dishonesty. Replicating Experiment 2 and providing additional support for the intergroup coalitional dishonesty hypothesis, the proportion of correct guesses in the ingroup condition (69.1%) was significantly higher than in the outgroup condition in Experiment 3 (58.5%), χ 2 (1, N = 1,189) = 14.58, p < .001, OR = 1.59, 95% CI [1.25, 2.02]. This effect of 10.6 percentage points corresponds to participants being 18.2% more likely to report correct guesses to benefit an ingroup member. Self-reported correct guesses in the outgroup coalitional condition (58.5%) were above chance (p < .001), indicating some willingness to lie even for outgroup members, though significantly less than for ingroup members.

Selfish vs. coalitional dishonesty.

A logistic regression with dishonesty type (selfish = 0, coalitional = 1) and target condition (outgroup = 0, ingroup = 1) as predictors revealed a significant interaction, b = 0.36, SE = 0.18, z = 2.00, p = .046, OR = 1.43, 95% CI [1.01, 2.04], demonstrating that intergroup bias was stronger in coalitional than selfish dishonesty (see Figure 4). Party-level differences. Neither Democrats (φ < .01, p = .905) nor Republicans (φ = .04, p = .340) showed intergroup bias in selfish dishonesty; the Party × Condition interaction was not significant (χ²(1) = 0.34, p = .559). For coalitional dishonesty, Democrats showed significant intergroup bias (68.3% vs. 52.3%, χ²(1) = 15.94, p < .001, φ = .16), while Republicans showed a directionally consistent but non-significant effect (69.9% vs. 65.2%, χ²(1) = 1.46, p = .227, φ = .05). The Party × Condition interaction was not statistically significant (p = .059). See Figure 5.

Figure 5. Proportion of reported correct guesses across dishonesty type (selfish vs. coalitional), target (ingroup vs. outgroup), and participant party affiliation (Democrat vs. Republican) (Experiment 3, N = 2,343). Democrats showed significant intergroup bias in coalitional dishonesty, while Republicans showed a directionally consistent but non-significant effect; neither party showed intergroup bias in selfish dishonesty, and the Party × Condition interaction was not significant in either dishonesty type. Dashed lines indicate the chance-level probability of correctly guessing a future die roll being odd or even (50%). Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.

Dishonesty beliefs.

Replicating Experiments 1 and 2, the difference between the estimated and actual rate of dishonest behavior of outgroup members (M = 12.53, SD = 29.00) was significantly higher than that of ingroup members (M = 4.76, SD = 27.70), t(2342) = 11.67, p < .001, d = 0.24, 95% CI [0.20, 0.28]. An exploratory 2 (Affiliation) × 2 (Behavioral Condition) × 2 (Dishonesty Type) × 2 (Belief Target: ingroup vs. outgroup, within-subjects) mixed ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of belief target, F(1, 2335) = 179.51, p < .001, η²p = .071, and a significant Belief Target × Affiliation interaction, F(1, 2335) = 39.41, p < .001, η²p = .017.

Both Democrats (d = 0.12) and Republicans (d = 0.38) overestimated outgroup dishonesty more than ingroup dishonesty, with Republicans showing a larger bias. Critically, the Belief Target × Condition × Dishonesty interaction was significant, F(1, 2335) = 22.47, p < .001, η²p = .010, indicating that the intergroup belief bias depended on the combination of behavioral condition and dishonesty type. See Figure 6. The four-way interaction with affiliation was not significant (F(1, 2335) = 0.08, p = .782), indicating that this pattern did not differ by party (see Supplemental Materials, Tables F4-F6, for all cell means and decompositions).

EXPERIMENT 4: ORGANIZATIONAL IDENTIFICATION AND COALITIONAL DISHONESTY

To test whether coalitional dishonesty generalizes beyond partisan identities and the context of American politics, this pre-registered experiment examined whether organizational identification increases the willingness to engage in dishonest behavior that benefits one's company at no personal gain. Unlike Experiments 1-3, which varied whether the victim or beneficiary was a political ingroup or outgroup member, Experiment 4 varied how strongly participants identified with the group that would benefit, which was described as the organization one was working for (with either high or low organizational identification). We used a scenariobased measure of dishonest intentions to examine whether organizational identification causally increases employees' willingness to engage in dishonest behavior that benefits their company at no personal gain, the potential role of moral disengagement in such coalitional dishonesty, and whether organizational threat amplifies the effect-expecting that threats to group outcomes could heighten the salience of group identity and further increase the motivation to act dishonestly on the group's behalf.

The hypotheses, design, sample size, exclusion criteria, and analyses were pre-registered (see https://aspredicted.org/v93ae2.pdf) before data collection. No deviations from the preregistration occurred. Exploratory analyses not included in the pre-registration are clearly labeled in the manuscript.

Method

Participants and power. We recruited 900 U.S.-based workers (full-time, part-time, or actively job-seeking) via Prolific. As pre-registered, we excluded participants who failed the visual perception bot check (n = 34), leaving a final sample of 866 participants (Mage = 41.05, SD = 12.76; 432 male, 408 female, 20 other, 6 undisclosed). A sensitivity analysis using G*POWER indicated that the achieved sample size could detect an effect size of f = .10 or larger with 80% power at α = .05. Procedure and measures. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions in a 2 (Organizational Identification: High vs. Low) × 2 (Organizational Threat: Threat vs.

Neutral) between-subjects design. We adapted the paradigm and measures from Study 3 of Chen et al. (2016), with pre-registration, a larger sample (N = 866), organizational threat as a moderator, a three-item unethical pro-organizational behavior (UPB) measure, and latent SEM mediation tests.

First, participants imagined they were the Marketing Director at a large retail company where they had worked for three years. In the high [low] identification condition, participants read that the company was a great [poor] fit, that they shared similar [very different] attitudes with coworkers about the company's direction, and that they felt a strong [did not feel a] sense of belonging and identification. After reading the vignette, participants responded to a two-item manipulation check of identification ("I would feel strongly identified with this company"; "I would feel a part of this company";1 = Strongly Disagree to7 = Strongly Agree; α = .99).

Participants then read a scenario in which their lowest-performing directly reporting employee, Tom, had applied to a rival company, whose HR manager requested a personal evaluation. The choice would not affect participants personally, but could substantially benefit the organization by offloading their lowest performer. In the threat condition, participants additionally read that the company faced significant financial pressure and that Tom's departure would free up resources. The scenario presented a choice between an honest negative evaluation, which would likely cost Tom the job, and an exaggerated positive recommendation that would ensure Tom gets hired by the rival. = 0.80) than those in the low identification condition (M = 1.64, SD = 1.13), t(864) = 72.36, p < .001, d = 4.92. Participants in the threat condition also reported significantly higher perceived organizational threat (M = 4.77, SD = 1.62) than those in the neutral condition (M = 2.42, SD = 1.60), t(864) = 21.49, p < .001, d = 1.46.

Unethical pro-organizational behavior.

As the main hypothesis, we predicted that organizational identification would increase willingness to engage in dishonest behavior that benefits the company at no personal gain, representing ingroup-favoring coalitional dishonesty in an organizational context. Consistent with this prediction, a 2 (Identification: High vs. Low) × 2 (Context: Threat vs. Neutral) between-subjects ANOVA on unethical pro-organizational behavior revealed a significant main effect of organizational identification, F(1, 862) = 22.63, p < .001, η²p = .026. Specifically, participants in the high identification condition reported higher dishonesty intentions (M = 3.28, SD = 1.92) than those in the low identification condition (M = 2.66, SD = 1.82). The main effect of threat context was not significant, F(1, 862) = 1.82, p = .177, η²p = .002, nor was the Identification × Context interaction, F(1, 862) = 0.05, p = .818, η²p < .001.

Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons revealed that the identification effect was significant in both the neutral condition (High: M = 3.20, SD = 1.92 vs. Low: M = 2.57, SD = 1.70), t(862) = 3.55, p = .002, d = 0.34, 95% CI [0.15, 0.53], and the threat condition (High: M = 3.35, SD = 1.92 vs. Low: M = 2.77, SD = 1.95), t(862) = 3.18, p = .008, d = 0.31, 95% CI [0.12, 0.50]. These results support our hypothesis that organizational identification increases coalitional dishonesty intentions, but not our prediction that organizational threat would amplify this effect. See Figure 7. Moral disengagement. We predicted that organizational identification would also increase moral disengagement from truth-telling norms-a cognitive process through which the perceived moral cost of dishonesty can be reduced. Consistent with this prediction, a 2 × 2 ANOVA on moral disengagement revealed a significant main effect of organizational identification, F(1, 862) = 33.42, p < .001, η²p = .037. Participants in the high identification condition reported higher moral disengagement from truth-telling in the workplace hiring scenario (M = 3.79, SD = 1.80) than those in the low identification condition (M = 3.07, SD = 1.75). The main effect of context was also significant, F(1, 862) = 5.31, p = .021, η²p = .006, with higher moral disengagement in the threat (M = 3.61) than neutral (M = 3.27) condition. The Identification × Context interaction was not significant, F(1, 862) = 0.14, p = .712, η²p < .001.

Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons revealed that the identification effect on moral disengagement was significant in both the neutral condition (High: M = 3.62, SD = 1.80 vs. Low: M = 2.96, SD = 1.65), t(862) = 3.85, p < .001, d = 0.37, 95% CI [0.18, 0.56], and the threat condition (High: M = 3.94, SD = 1.80 vs. Low: M = 3.20, SD = 1.86), t(862) = 4.32, p < .001, d = 0.42, 95% CI [0.23, 0.61]. These results support our hypothesis that organizational identification increases moral disengagement, but not our prediction that threat would amplify this effect.

Mediation.

As an exploration of the decision process, we predicted that moral disengagement would mediate the effect of organizational identification on unethical proorganizational behavior (UPB). A latent factor moderated mediation model using structural equation modeling with bootstrapped confidence intervals (1,000 resamples) showed that the indirect effect of organizational identification on UPB through moral disengagement was significant in both the neutral (ab = 0.54, 95% BCa CI [0.26, 0.82]) and threat (ab = 0.60, 95% BCa CI [0.31, 0.89]) conditions. The index of moderated mediation was not significant (0.07, 95% BCa CI [-0.33, 0.46]), indicating that moral disengagement mediated the identification effect on UPB regardless of organizational threat. These results support our prediction that moral disengagement mediates the identification-dishonesty link, but not that organizational threat strengthens it further as a moderator.

GENERAL DISCUSSION

In the current research, four experiments (N = 6,096) revealed an unpredicted asymmetry in intergroup bias in moral decision-making: While people lied more to benefit an ingroup than an outgroup member despite receiving no personal benefits themselves, they lied at similar rates to increase their own earnings at the cost of an outgroup member as an ingroup member. That is, we found robust support for intergroup bias in coalitional dishonesty but no evidence for intergroup bias in selfish dishonesty.

Theoretical Contributions

Our research offers five contributions to the literature on social identity and moral decision-making. First, we reveal that while intergroup bias did not emerge for personally benefiting selfish dishonesty, it robustly emerged for other-benefiting coalitional dishonesty.

These results are consistent with recent research finding that the effect of observing unethical others on one's own dishonest behavior did not vary across ingroup or outgroup-signaling others (Martuza & Aslan, 2026), and earlier findings of ingroup-favoring pro-social lying often conditional on region, season, or age (Aksoy & Palma, 2019; Cadsby et al., 2016; Michailidou & Rotondi, 2019; Sierksma et al., 2019). Consistent with recent theorizing about the contextual nature of human morality (Del Rosario et al., 2024; Earp et al., 2021), the moral cost of lying seems to vary systematically across the group identity of the beneficiary, creating a robust form of coalitional dishonesty. Second, we observed a surprising asymmetry in how social identity shapes the two different types of intergroup bias. Unlike our consistent finding of intergroup bias in coalitional dishonesty, we repeatedly observed no effect on selfish intergroup dishonesty. One interpretation of this asymmetry is that social identity shapes the moral cost of lying more strongly in the context of selfless dishonesty benefiting the ingroup versus outgroup than in the context of selfish dishonesty at the expense of the ingroup versus outgroup. Thus, we identify a boundary condition for intergroup bias in moral decision-making, with social identity shaping dishonesty that benefits others, but not dishonesty that benefits oneself.

Third, the finding that intergroup bias in coalitional dishonesty emerged even when there was no opportunity to reduce an outgroup member's earnings (Experiment 2), meaning people lied more when it could simply improve the earnings of an ingroup member without affecting the earnings of any outgroup member, suggests that intergroup dishonesty might not require a competitive or hostile function. Thus, intergroup bias in coalitional dishonesty is likely driven by "ingroup love" rather than "outgroup hate", consistent with prior work finding people are reluctant to actively harm outgroup members (Weisel & Böhm, 2015).

Fourth, Experiment 4 conceptually replicated intergroup bias in coalitional dishonesty in a workplace scenario-based context, finding that stronger organizational identification increases the intention to lie for the organization. Further, the effect of organizational identification on these intentions was mediated by moral disengagement from truth-telling norms (Chen et al., 2016), offering suggestive evidence that greater moral disengagement, which we interpret as reflecting a lower perceived moral cost of lying, partly explains coalitional dishonesty in the workplace.

Fifth, when comparing beliefs with actual behavior in the same experimental situation, we found that participants generally overestimated outgroup dishonesty more than ingroup dishonesty, even though intergroup bias emerged only in coalitional dishonesty and not selfish dishonesty. This finding extends research on biased perceptions of political outgroups (Lees & Cikara, 2019; Puryear et al., 2024) and overestimation of others' dishonesty in general (Martuza et al., 2026), by demonstrating that laypeople cannot accurately predict how intergroup bias actually shapes real dishonest behavior, believing outgroup misbehavior is much more common than it really is.

Practical Implications

Our research offers two main practical implications. First, our findings reveal a specific vulnerability in polarized societies and institutions: Dishonesty may arise not only from individual greed, but also from actions that advantage one's group. Also, while strong organizational identification has many other benefits, employees who identify strongly with their organization seem more willing to selflessly lie on its behalf. Thus, integrity management systems may need to consider deterrents for group-serving dishonesty, and not only focus on selfish dishonesty in the traditional sense.

Second, for polarized societies, the gap between beliefs and actual behavior reveals both a risk factor and an intervention target. Misperceptions of outgroup dishonesty may rationalize defensive misconduct ("they would do it to us") and sustain cycles of reciprocal distrust.

Correcting such biased beliefs about outgroup dishonesty may help attenuate group tensions and prevent group-serving misconduct from escalating.

Limitations and Future Research

Our research has several limitations, offering directions for future research. First, Experiments 1-3 studied partisan identities of U.S. participants. Because partisan identities are strongly moralized (Finkel et al., 2020), the coalitional dishonesty we observe might be larger than in weaker groups. Future research should examine whether the present findings extend to other social identities and cultural contexts, and whether coalitional dishonesty similarly emerges in minimal group settings. Second, we focused on comparing aggregate dishonesty rates across experimental conditions, and did not observe individual-level lying. Future research could use paradigms that allow for the observation of individual dishonest choices as well.

Third, the die-roll paradigm measures binary dishonesty choices rather than levels of dishonesty. Future research could investigate whether the extent of intergroup bias differs across smaller versus larger acts of dishonesty. Fourth, while our designs isolate selfish and coalitional motives, real-world dishonesty can involve more complex trade-offs in which individual material gains, group interests, and truth-telling motives may interact. Future research could vary personal gain and partner loss separately, and compare lying with other ways of helping the ingroup.

Fifth, the behavioral studies involved relatively modest financial stakes ($0.75), which for practical reasons are common in psychology and behavioral social science. Future research could test whether the observed patterns replicate under conditions involving larger incentives and more consequential outcomes. Sixth, Experiment 4 used hypothetical organizational identities with self-reported measures, and used correlational mediation as suggestive process evidence.

Future research could examine coalitional dishonesty in real organizations and use experimental designs for causal-chain process evidence.

Finally, given the importance of reducing publication bias (Sterling, 1959) and learning from informative null findings rather than discounting them (Chopra et al., 2024), we encourage future work on intergroup moral decision-making to consider both our positive finding (intergroup bias in coalitional dishonesty) and null finding (no evidence for intergroup bias in selfish dishonesty) when further examining the conditions under which social identity might or might not shape moral decision-making.

Conclusion

Across four pre-registered experiments, we find evidence of intergroup bias in coalitional dishonesty but not in selfish dishonesty. People lie more to benefit an ingroup than an outgroup

Our research was partially funded by the Centre of Ethics and Economics and the Centre for Experimental Research on Fairness, Inequality and Rationality at the Norwegian School of Economics.

After reading the scenario, participants responded to three moral disengagement items (Bandura, 2002; Chen et al., 2016) measuring the perceived acceptability of dishonesty to protect company interests ("It would be ok to be misleading to protect my company's interests"; "It would be ok to withhold potentially damaging information to protect my company's interests"; "It would be ok to be less than fully truthful to protect my company's interests";1 = Strongly Disagree to7 = Strongly Agree; α = .94). We consider this measure as a self-reported proxy for the moral cost of lying, assuming that greater moral disengagement reflects a lower perceived moral cost.

Then, participants responded to three unethical pro-organizational behavior (UPB) items measuring the likelihood of writing an exaggerated recommendation letter for Tom ("How likely would you be to write a glowing recommendation letter for Tom that exaggerates his abilities?" ; "How likely would you be to write a glowing recommendation letter for Tom that exaggerates his performance?" ; "How likely would you be to write a glowing recommendation letter for Tom that exaggerates his potential?" ;1 = Very Unlikely to7 = Very Likely; α = .98). Both scales were averaged to form composites. Participants then responded to a single-item threat manipulation check (1 = Not at all Threatened to7 = Extremely Threatened), a visual perception bot check, social dominance orientation (SDO; 8 items; α = .92; Ho et al., 2015), moralistic response tendencies (6 items; α = .76; Steenkamp et al., 2010), and demographics (age, gender, education, income, political orientation).

Manipulation checks.

Both manipulations were successful. Participants in the high identification condition reported significantly higher organizational identification (M = 6.46, SD member, even when they receive no personal benefit. When truth-telling conflicts with loyalty, dishonesty can become a way to be a "good" group member. Thus, integrity failures in polarized societies and organizations can arise from coalitional motives as well as individual greed.

Reducing the salience of group boundaries or correcting inflated beliefs about outgroup dishonesty may help preserve truth-telling norms and rebuild mutual trust.
